title: Adonais: occasion and publication
short: Shelley's elegy for Keats, who died in Rome on 23 February 1821, was written at Pisa in spring 1821 and printed there in July.
body: Shelley learned of Keats's death in April 1821 and wrote the poem in the following weeks; it was printed at Pisa in the types of Didot and dated July 1821. The Preface (not printed in this archive) blames Keats's decline on the 'savage criticism' of Endymion in the Quarterly Review (April 1818), a review traditionally attributed to John Wilson Croker (the attribution is not entirely certain), and praises Joseph Severn, who nursed Keats in Rome. The theory that a review killed Keats was mistaken, since he died of tuberculosis, but it shapes the poem's attack on the critic. The two poets had met through Leigh Hunt but were never close. The poem opens with the refrain-cry of Greek pastoral elegy.

title: The name 'Adonais'
short: A coinage from Adonis, the beautiful youth mourned by Venus in Greek elegy, perhaps blended with Hebrew Adonai, 'Lord'.
body: Adonis, beloved of Aphrodite, was killed by a boar; his annual mourning was a fertility rite, and Bion's Lament for Adonis begins with the cry 'I wail for Adonis'. The form 'Adonais' is Shelley's own; many critics also hear the Hebrew Adonai, 'my Lord', a title of God, which fits the poem's movement from mourning a dead youth to celebrating a soul made one with the Eternal. The opening line closely imitates Bion's refrain.

title: Pastoral elegy in Spenserian stanzas
short: Fifty-five Spenserian stanzas follow the conventions of pastoral elegy: lament, procession of mourners, attack on the guilty, and final consolation.
body: The poem joins Greek pastoral elegy (Bion's Lament for Adonis; the Lament for Bion attributed to Moschus, quoted in Shelley's epigraph) with the English line of Spenser's Astrophel and Milton's Lycidas. Its 495 lines use Spenser's nine-line stanza. Its structure follows the genre: invocation and lament (st. 1-17), the mother's grief (18-29), the procession of poets (30-35), invective against the reviewer (36-38), and a consolation in which the mourners' grief is reversed (39-55). Critics differ on whether that ending is a Platonic triumph or a desire for death.

title: Urania
short: Keats's mourning mother is Urania: Aphrodite Urania, heavenly Love, in place of Venus mourning Adonis, and also the Muse whom Milton invoked.
body: In Bion, Aphrodite mourns Adonis. Shelley replaces her with Urania, a figure of two traditions: Aphrodite Urania, the 'heavenly' Venus who in Plato's Symposium stands for spiritual love, and Urania the Muse of astronomy, whom Milton invoked as his heavenly muse in Paradise Lost book 7. Thus Keats is the son of spiritual Beauty and of the sublime Muse of English epic. Urania is 'lorn' (forsaken) and 'sate' (sat) in her Paradise while he died: the gods failed to protect him. She is roused in stanzas 22-29.

anchor: pierced by the shaft which flies
title: The shaft that flies in darkness
short: The arrow is the anonymous review; the phrasing may recall the 'arrow that flieth by day' and the 'pestilence that walketh in darkness' of Psalm 91.
body: Psalm 91:5-6 promises the righteous that they will not fear 'the arrow that flieth by day; nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness'. Shelley's shaft is the anonymous review, which strikes unseen. The image fits the Adonis myth of a youth killed by a wound and anticipates the Preface's claim that the review led to Keats's death. It also prepares the image of Byron as Apollo the archer (st. 28).

anchor: the Sire of an immortal strain
title: Milton, 'third among the sons of light'
short: Stanza 4 describes Milton, blind and old after the Restoration of 1660; Shelley ranks him third of the great epic poets, after Homer and Dante.
body: Milton was 'Blind, old and lonely' when the monarchy was restored in 1660 and the 'priest, the slave, and the liberticide' (destroyer of liberty) triumphed with their 'loathed rite / Of lust and blood', Shelley's hostile view of the Restoration and the executions of the regicides. In A Defence of Poetry, written the same year, Shelley calls Homer the first and Dante the second epic poet and Milton the third. Urania as Milton's muse thus mourns two sons. The stanza makes the elegy political as well as literary.

title: Echo, Hyacinth and Narcissus
short: Nature mourns through Ovidian figures: Echo, who pined into a mere voice for Narcissus, and the flowers Hyacinth and Narcissus.
body: In Metamorphoses 3, the nymph Echo, rejected by Narcissus, wastes away until only her voice remains; Narcissus, in love with his reflection, becomes a flower. In book 10, Apollo (Phoebus) accidentally kills his beloved Hyacinthus, from whose blood springs the hyacinth. Shelley's 'pathetic fallacy' makes Echo refuse to answer any sound but Keats's songs, and Spring throw down her buds as if she were Autumn. The figures of Echo and of Narcissus are also figures of self-absorption and of art as imitation, which some critics see as part of the poem's self-questioning.

title: The eagle and Albion
short: The eagle that renews its 'mighty youth' in the sun recalls Milton's Areopagitica image of England as an eagle; 'Albion' is England.
body: In Areopagitica (1644) Milton imagines England as an eagle 'mewing her mighty youth' and kindling her eyes at the noonday sun; the belief that eagles renew themselves by flying near the sun goes back to Psalm 103:5 ('thy youth is renewed like the eagle's') and bestiary lore. Shelley's echo again links Keats with Milton and makes England (Albion) the chief mourner. The stanza ends by calling down 'the curse of Cain', the first murderer (Genesis 4:11-12), on the reviewer.

title: "Nought we know, dies": the turn to doubt
short: Spring's renewal raises the poem's central question: matter is never lost, but must the mind alone perish, like a sword consumed before its sheath?
body: Stanzas 18-21 contrast the returning spring with the dead poet. Shelley states a principle of conservation: nothing that we know dies, but changes form, as a corpse 'Exhales itself in flowers'. The question follows whether the knowing mind is the one thing destroyed, like a blade burnt by lightning while its scabbard survives. The 'intense atom' of consciousness glows and is quenched. Stanza 21 continues in doubt ('Whence are we, and why are we?'). These questions are answered only in the poem's final third, which is why critics treat the elegy as an argument rather than a simple lament.

title: The mirrored shield and the dragon
short: Urania asks why Keats did not wait until he had the weapons of maturity, like Perseus with Athena's mirror-shield, before facing the dragon of criticism.
body: Perseus killed the Gorgon Medusa by looking only at her reflection in the polished shield of Athena, goddess of wisdom. Urania wishes Keats had carried 'Wisdom the mirrored shield' and 'scorn the spear'. The 'unpastured dragon' (the hungry, untamed beast) is the hostile literary world. 'The full cycle' and 'crescent sphere' compare the poet to a waxing moon not yet full. Shelley may also have recalled Keats's own preface to Endymion, which called the poem the work of youthful immaturity.

title: The Pythian of the age: Byron
short: Byron is the Apollo of his age, who slew the critical Python with one arrow, English Bards and Scotch Reviewers (1809).
body: Apollo was called Pythian after killing the serpent Python at Delphi (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.438-451). Byron answered the Edinburgh Review's mockery of his first volume with the satire English Bards and Scotch Reviewers (1809), after which, Shelley suggests, the reviewers fawned on him. Wolves, ravens and vultures are the predatory critics, who attack only the weak. The contrast highlights Keats's defencelessness.

title: The Pilgrim of Eternity; Ierne's lyrist
short: The mountain shepherds are contemporary poets: Byron, author of Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, and Thomas Moore, Ireland's ('Ierne's') singer.
body: The procession of shepherd-poets is a pastoral convention (compare the mourners in Lycidas). Byron is the 'Pilgrim of Eternity', after his Childe Harold's Pilgrimage; his fame is 'An early but enduring monument'. 'Ierne' is a classical name for Ireland, and its 'sweetest lyrist' is Thomas Moore, whose Irish Melodies (1808-34) mourned Ireland's 'saddest wrong', its subjection to England. Joseph Severn's own copy, now in the Morgan Library, is marked at passages on the mourners.

title: The frail Form: Shelley's self-portrait
short: Shelley paints himself as the last, neglected mourner, an Actaeon hunted by his own thoughts: one of the most debated passages of self-dramatising in Romantic verse.
body: Actaeon, the hunter who saw the goddess Diana bathing, was turned into a stag and torn apart by his own hounds (Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.138-252). Shelley, who has 'gazed on Nature's naked loveliness', is pursued by his thoughts like hounds. The figure is 'a phantom among men' who sings 'in the accents of an unknown land'. Critics are divided: some find the portrait moving and self-aware, others self-pitying (Victorian readers often complained). It anticipates the ending, where the poet himself moves toward death.

title: Pardlike Spirit; the thyrsus
short: A 'pard' is a leopard, the beast of Dionysus; the poet's spear twined with ivy and topped with a cone is the Dionysian thyrsus.
body: Leopards drew the chariot of Dionysus (Bacchus), god of inspiration, and his worshippers carried the thyrsus, a wand topped with a pine cone and wreathed in ivy. Shelley's version has a cypress cone, the cypress being the tree of mourning. His wreath of pansies (for thought, as in Hamlet 4.5) and faded violets makes the self-portrait an emblem of inspired weakness: 'A Power / Girt round with weakness'. The deer 'struck by the hunter's dart' echoes Cowper's description of himself in The Task (book 3) as 'a stricken deer, that left the herd'.

title: "like Cain's or Christ's"
short: The poet's 'branded and ensanguined brow' resembles either the mark of Cain, the outcast murderer, or the thorn-crowned brow of Christ.
body: Genesis 4:15 records that God set a mark on Cain; the Gospels tell of Christ's crown of thorns (Matthew 27:29). The double comparison expresses an ambivalence about the poet as outcast: guilty exile or innocent martyr. Shelley, expelled from Oxford for atheism and cast out by English society, seems to accept both roles. The last half-line, 'oh! that it should be so!', shows him unsure which applies. Readers have found the comparison to Christ either daring or presumptuous.

title: The nameless worm: the reviewer
short: The anonymous reviewer of Endymion is a 'deaf and viperous murderer', a 'noteless blot on a remembered name', whose punishment is to remain himself.
body: Quarterly reviews were unsigned; the hostile review of Endymion (April 1818) is traditionally attributed to John Wilson Croker, though Shelley wrongly suspected Robert Southey (writing to Leigh Hunt in December 1818) after first thinking of William Gifford. Shelley's curse is ironic: 'Live thou', with 'Remorse and Self-contempt'. This invective is a convention of pastoral elegy (St Peter's speech against corrupt clergy in Lycidas) but sharpened into personal satire. The stanzas' violence troubled some contemporaries, and the Preface's story that the review killed Keats was mocked by Byron in Don Juan (canto 11, st. 60), where the mind is 'snuff'd out by an article'.

title: "Dust to the dust!": the burning fountain
short: The burial service's 'dust to dust' applies to the body only; the spirit flows back to the 'burning fountain' from which it came.
body: The Book of Common Prayer's burial rite commits the body 'earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust', echoing Genesis 3:19. Shelley adds a Platonic idea: the soul is a 'portion of the Eternal', a spark returning to a fiery source, which 'must glow / Through time and change'. The image of fire continues in the reviewer's 'cold embers' choking 'the sordid hearth of shame'. The stanza is the hinge between lament and consolation.

anchor: Peace, peace! he is not dead
title: "Peace, peace! he is not dead"
short: The great reversal: it is the living who dream and decay; the dead poet 'hath awakened from the dream of life'.
body: Stanza 39 turns the poem's imagery inside out. Life is now the dream and the 'stormy visions' of fear and grief; the mourners are 'corpses in a charnel'. Shelley echoes Hamlet's 'To sleep, perchance to dream' and Calderon's Life is a Dream, a play he admired, as well as Plato's cave. 'He has outsoared the shadow of our night' (st. 40) makes him free of 'Envy and calumny'. 'Mourn not for Adonais' (st. 41) reverses the opening refrain, so the elegy's formal structure is a reversal of 'weep for Adonais'.

anchor: He is made one with Nature
title: "He is made one with Nature": the plastic stress
short: Adonais becomes part of the shaping Power of the world; critics debate whether this is pantheism, Platonism, or merely the body returning to nature.
body: Stanzas 42-43 suggest a world-soul, a 'Power' that 'wields the world with never-wearied love', and in which Keats now shares, his voice heard in thunder and the nightingale (an allusion to Keats's own ode). The 'one Spirit's plastic stress' is a shaping pressure ('plastic' means formative) that drives the dull 'dross' of matter toward its own likeness. The idea recalls Wordsworth's 'Tintern Abbey' and Coleridge's 'plastic' breeze in 'The Eolian Harp'. Some critics see a Neoplatonic emanation; others note that stanza 43 implies a struggle of spirit against resistant matter, so the consolation is only partial.

title: Chatterton, Sidney, Lucan
short: The 'inheritors of unfulfilled renown' are poets who died young: Thomas Chatterton (d. 1770, aged 17), Sir Philip Sidney (d. 1586, 31) and Lucan (d. AD 65, 25).
body: Chatterton, the 'marvellous boy' of the Rowley forgeries, killed himself in London at seventeen; the Romantics made him the type of neglected genius. Sidney, poet and soldier, died of a wound at Zutphen; his 'Sublimely mild' character, which Spenser elegised in Astrophel, makes him a model of the gentle poet. Lucan, author of the Pharsalia (De Bello Civili) on the war of Caesar and Pompey, was forced to kill himself after joining the Pisonian conspiracy against Nero. Tacitus reports that as he bled to death he recited his own verses on a dying soldier; 'by his death approved' implies that his death proved his integrity.

title: "Thou art become as one of us"; Vesper
short: The dead poets welcome Keats to a vacant star, as the dead kings greet the King of Babylon in Isaiah 14; he becomes Vesper, the evening star.
body: Isaiah 14:9-10 shows the dead rising from their thrones to greet the fallen King of Babylon: 'Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us?' Genesis 3:22 has God say 'the man is become as one of us'. Shelley turns a mocking welcome into a glorious one: the poets give Keats a 'kingless sphere' among the stars. Vesper (Hesperus), the evening star, is also the morning star; the Greek epigraph from Plato that heads the poem (not printed here) plays on that double star, Aster.

title: Rome, the sepulchre of our joy
short: Rome, where 'ages, empires and religions' lie buried, is the grave not of Keats but of our joy; the poets lend glory to Rome rather than borrowing it.
body: Shelley turns the Romantic topos of Rome's ruins (Byron's Childe Harold canto 4, 1818) to the poet's advantage. Empires were built by those 'who made the world their prey'; poets 'waged contention with their time's decay'. Rome is 'at once the Paradise, / The grave, the city, and the wilderness', a summary of the elegy's own moods. The mourner is led to 'a slope of green access' covered with flowers: the Protestant Cemetery, which Shelley had described in the Preface as romantic and lonely.

title: The pyramid of Cestius and the cemetery
short: The pyramid tomb of Gaius Cestius (c. 12 BC) stands beside Rome's Protestant Cemetery, where Keats was buried and where Shelley's son William already lay.
body: Gaius Cestius, a Roman magistrate, built himself a marble-faced pyramid as a tomb ('This refuge for his memory'), later absorbed into the Aurelian walls ('gray walls moulder round'). Beside it lies the Protestant (non-Catholic) Cemetery, the 'camp of death' of 'a newer band'. Shelley's three-year-old son William had been buried there in 1819, so 'these graves are all too young' (st. 51) carries a private grief. Shelley's own ashes were buried there in 1823.

title: The One and the many; the dome of glass
short: The most famous stanza: life is a 'dome of many-coloured glass' staining the 'white radiance of Eternity' until death breaks it.
body: The Platonic contrast of the eternal One and the changing many is expressed in an image of light: eternity is white (all colours together), and life refracts it into colours, as a stained-glass dome does. The image is beautiful but ambivalent. Life's colours are a 'stain', a falsification, yet they are also what makes the light visible. Death 'tramples' the dome to fragments. Then comes the command 'Die, / If thou wouldst be with that which thou dost seek!', which some read as Neoplatonic transcendence and others as a wish for death, troubling given Shelley's drowning a year later.

title: The spirit's bark: the ending
short: The poet's own soul is swept out to sea by the 'breath' he once invoked, toward Adonais shining as a star 'where the Eternal are'.
body: The 'breath whose might I have invoked in song' recalls Shelley's 'Ode to the West Wind' (1819), with its prayer 'Make me thy lyre'. Now the wind drives his 'bark' (small boat) far from the 'trembling throng' who never risk the storm, and the solid world is 'riven'. The final image of Keats as a star fulfils the epigraph and stanza 46. Readers have often noted the uncanny foreshadowing of Shelley's drowning in his boat in the Gulf of Spezia in July 1822. The plural 'the Eternal are' implies a community of immortal souls.
